questiontext.text: What are the three actions in the skeleton of every backtracking function?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. We choose an option, explore what follows with a recursive call, then undo the option so the next one can be tried.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void f(int n) {
    if (n == 0) {
        return;
    }
    cout << n << " ";
    f(n - 1);
    cout << n << " ";
}

int main() {
    f(3);
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The first cout runs on the way down (3, 2, 1). When n reaches 0 the calls start returning, and the second cout runs on the way up in reverse order (1, 2, 3).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: How many subsets does a set of 6 items have (counting the empty one)?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Every item is either in or out, so there are 2^6 = 64 subsets. The number 720 is 6!, the number of arrangements.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int cnt = 0;

void go(int i, int taken) {
    if (i == 3) {
        if (taken == 2) {
            cnt++;
        }
        return;
    }
    go(i + 1, taken + 1);
    go(i + 1, taken);
}

int main() {
    go(0, 0);
    cout << cnt << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The program counts the leaves in which exactly two of the three items were taken. Those are {1,2}, {1,3} and {2,3}, so the answer is 3.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps of a backtracking function.

Drag the steps into the correct order.

1. [[1]]

2. [[2]]

3. [[3]]

4. [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The base case is checked first. Then we choose, explore, and finally undo, which restores the state for the next option.

The correct answer:

  1. Check whether the solution is complete (base case)
  2. Choose: add an option to the partial solution
  3. Explore: call the function again for the next decision
  4. Undo: remove the option you added

questiontext.text: Why must the line used[v] = false; come after the recursive call when we build arrangements?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. It is the undo. If the mark stayed, the number would look "used" in every later branch and many arrangements would never be found.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: So the number becomes available again for other branches
Because the compiler requires the order

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int n = 3, k = 0;
vector<int> cur;
bool used[4];

void build() {
    if ((int)cur.size() == n) {
        k++;
        if (k == 4) {
            for (int x : cur) {
                cout << x << " ";
            }
            cout << endl;
        }
        return;
    }
    for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++) {
        if (used[v]) {
            continue;
        }
        used[v] = true;
        cur.push_back(v);
        build();
        cur.pop_back();
        used[v] = false;
    }
}

int main() {
    build();
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The arrangements come out in ascending order: 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321. The fourth one is 2 3 1.

        if (used[v]) {
            continue;
        }
        used[v] = true;
        cur.push_back(v);
        build();
        cur.[[1]];
        used[v] = [[2]];

int main() {
    build();
    cout << cnt << endl;

generalfeedback.text:

questiontext.text: A program tries to cut a branch when sum > target. When is this cut valid?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. With positive numbers the sum can only grow, so once it passes the target nothing below can fix it. With negative numbers a later item could bring the sum back down.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: When all the numbers are positive

questiontext.text:
Match each line of a backtracking program with its role.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

cur.push_back(v);  →  [[1]]

build();  →  [[2]]

cur.pop_back();  →  [[3]]

if (used[v]) continue;  →  [[4]]

if ((int)cur.size() == n)  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Every backtracking program is made of these five roles, in this order.

The correct answer:

  • cur.push_back(v); → Choose
  • build(); → Explore
  • cur.pop_back(); → Undo
  • if (used[v]) continue; → Skip a number already used
  • if ((int)cur.size() == n) → Detect a complete solution

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int a[] = {4, 3, 5};
int target = 5;
int calls = 0;

void walk(int i, int sum) {
    calls++;
    if (sum > target) {
        return;
    }
    if (i == 3) {
        return;
    }
    walk(i + 1, sum + a[i]);
    walk(i + 1, sum);
}

int main() {
    walk(0, 0);
    cout << calls << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Without the cut there would be 2^4 - 1 = 15 calls. The branch whose sum reaches 7 is stopped at once, which removes the two calls that would have been made below it, leaving 13.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Sort each situation: is cutting the branch valid? (all items are positive numbers unless stated)

Drag the correct label next to every item.

the sum already exceeds the target  →  [[1]]

a square is attacked by an earlier queen  →  [[1]]

a number is already used in this arrangement  →  [[1]]

negative numbers exist and the sum exceeds the target  →  [[2]]

only two items have been processed and the sum is below the target  →  [[2]]

the first item was skipped  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A cut is valid only when it is certain that no completion of the branch can succeed. Exceeding a target with positive numbers, an attacked square and a repeated number all make failure certain. Negative numbers, an unfinished list, or merely skipping an item do not.

The correct answer:

Valid cut: the sum already exceeds the target, a square is attacked by an earlier queen, a number is already used in this arrangement
Not a valid cut: negative numbers exist and the sum exceeds the target, only two items have been processed and the sum is below the target, the first item was skipped

questiontext.text:
How many leaves does the recursion tree have when each call branches into "take" and "leave" and there are 5 levels?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int leaves = 0;

void go(int i) {
    if (i == 5) {
        leaves++;
        return;
    }
    go(i + 1);
    go(i + 1);
}

int main() {
    go(0);
    cout << leaves << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Each level doubles the number of calls, so there are 2^5 = 32 leaves.

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Backtracking  →  [[1]]

Base case  →  [[2]]

Pruning  →  [[3]]

Partial solution  →  [[4]]

Permutation  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five words describe the whole technique: build, stop, skip, remember and order.

The correct answer:

  • Backtracking → Build a solution step by step and undo the last step
  • Base case → The case that stops the recursion
  • Pruning → Skipping a branch that cannot succeed
  • Partial solution → What has been built so far
  • Permutation → An ordering of all the items

questiontext.text:
Sort each line: does it run before the recursive call (choose) or after it (undo)?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

col[c] = true;  →  [[1]]

cur.push_back(v);  →  [[1]]

diagA[row + c] = true;  →  [[1]]

cur.pop_back();  →  [[2]]

used[v] = false;  →  [[2]]

col[c] = false;  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Marks and additions belong before the recursive call. Their exact opposites (removals and false marks) belong after it, so that the state is restored.

The correct answer:

Before the recursive call: col[c] = true;, cur.push_back(v);, diagA[row + c] = true;
After the recursive call: cur.pop_back();, used[v] = false;, col[c] = false;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int n = 3, cnt = 0;
bool col[3];

void rooks(int row) {
    if (row == 2) {
        cnt++;
        return;
    }
    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
        if (col[c]) {
            continue;
        }
        col[c] = true;
        rooks(row + 1);
        col[c] = false;
    }
}

int main() {
    rooks(0);
    cout << cnt << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The first rook has 3 free columns and the second has 2 left, so there are 3 x 2 = 6 ways to place two rooks that do not share a column.
